Pay attention to this particular question: the relation of Utopia to human nature.
Eventually, the manufacture of the homunculus.
In More there is still the classical humanist assumption about human nature.
In Defoe’s Robinson Crusoe, there is already the construction that begins from the isolated individual.
In Swift, human beings themselves are fantastically altered: giants, dwarfs, horses.
In Aldous Huxley, standardized human beings are deliberately manufactured by scientific means.
In other words, this is total planning. It includes even the natural facts of the human body and mind within its removal from place.

Utopia therefore means: the consistent uprooting of things from place in the most total sense possible, until even humanity’s own place within the nature that has so far been given to it is abolished.
The connection between order and location is broken.
Plato’s Republic is a Utopia insofar as every Idea represents a removal from concrete reality.

Pierre Linn had already shown in 1938 that the totalitarian state is the logically consistent ideal state: Platonically rather than Aristotelian-Thomistically consistent, once the difference between Idea and reality is settled in favour of the Idea and the Idea is made real. But Plato does not yet think in an exact scientific manner. Nor globally.
His thought still remains tied to place. Yet his idealism opens the road toward Utopia.
Again and again it is Aldous Huxley’s enormous, crushing, practically and theoretically overwhelming Brave New World that defines for us today both the idea of Utopia and the idea of the New World.
Thomas More brings the removal from place at the beginning of the geographical revolution of space.
Huxley brings the removal of humanity itself at the beginning of the technological revolution of space. For we are only now entering the age of technology.
More comes from the England that is preparing to conquer the new world of the sea.

Huxley comes from the point at which the modern industrial and technological world begins opening into a new world whose adventures will be greater and more terrible than those of the old adventurers of the pirate age of the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries.
(Then a question about the word: corny.)
So, my dear Max, nothing is above You.
Strictly speaking, your sentence “Nothing is above Me” cannot even survive translation into this form of addressing another person.
The I rejects such forms of address.
Being addressed as “you” already threatens it in its uniqueness.
Millions of us can shout together in chorus:
Perhaps you can say this about yourself. And perhaps millions who roar along in your chorus can say it too.
Unfortunately, all I can say about myself is that I do not know whether I am I, or whether nothing is above Me.
I do not know what this I of mine actually is.
Whether it is a fixed star or a will-o’-the-wisp in a swamp. Or both.
Are you one unique I? Or are there a thousand, countless selves inside your I? I know none of this. I do not know who I am.
If you know who you are, so much the better.
“Living, I consume myself.” I too consume myself. That much is certain.
My body consumes me and I consume my body. I do not know which of us is consuming the other.
You celebrate your I with jubilation.
Why do you show us only its euphoric, high-spirited side?
Surely your I has other sides too, you cheerful Euphorion of yourself.
In any event, good friend, I am gradually coming to know you, and I do not wish to interrupt your feast of life any longer.
What is remarkable about Max Stirner is not this philosophy. It is the desperation of his struggle against the frauds and ghosts of his age.
The honesty of this bankrupt ego, who does not call upon other people to liberate themselves so that he can place himself at their head;
who does not surrender himself to some substitute religion;
whose entire strength consists only in the weakness of everyone else.
The typical superiority of Brother Straubinger—to whom Stirner also belongs, as a boor, a swaggerer, a student roughneck—so long as this Brother does not try to become a leader but remains a drummer.

The totality of mobilization consists in this: even the unmoved mover of Aristotelian philosophy has now been set in motion and mobilized. Then the old separation between unmoving contemplation and moving activity comes to an end. The observer himself begins to move. And once that happens, he can no longer identify and prove the Ens perfectissimum, the most perfect being, with the old certainty. Then we are all activist observers and observing activists.
At most, one possibility remains imaginable: that in this way we might one day produce the Ens perfectissimum ourselves. Then the rule becomes:
Whoever is not on the road experiences nothing.
What is miserable about Machiavelli is the half-heartedness involved in speaking about power at all—turning power into an object of discussion.
Power is and remains a secret.
Public power is the most impenetrable secret of all.
Anyone who possesses power knows this.
Anyone who wants power ought to know it.
A consistent Machiavellian speaks like a Tolstoyan.
But a philosophy of the will to power is the summit of the most miserable bad taste and existential stupidity.
On Otto Veit’s efforts concerning “natural law”:
Compare the chain of antitheses on pp. 395–96 of issue 3 of Merkur, with positive law as the opposite term.
I regard concepts like these as revivals from legal history—perhaps even anachronistic revivals—produced by jurists philosophizing helplessly.
The distinction suited to our own time is: legality and legitimacy.
At the very beginning of his great speech on dictatorship of 4 January 1849, he attacks the politician Cortina for turning unconditional adherence to legality into a principle.
For Cortés, dictatorship is no longer legal, but it can be legitimate.
The age of unconditional legality is over.
The practical question is merely whether dictatorship will come from above or from below—today one would say from the Right or from the Left. So the real question is the legitimacy of dictatorship:

“When legality is enough to save society, legality; when legality is not enough, dictatorship.” And almost automatically, already in this speech of 1849, the corresponding concept appears: legitimacy.
“Dictatorship is a legitimate government like any other government.”
There is also a philosophically very important document showing that today’s real issue is precisely this opposition between legality and legitimacy.
In more than one respect, it is almost a classic document:
Georg Lukács’s essay “Legality and Illegality” of July 1920, which Lukács later included as a chapter in History and Class Consciousness (Malik-Verlag, Berlin, 1923, pp. 261–75).

Lukács says there—in agreement with Lenin’s work on left-wing radicalism as the childhood sickness of revolution—that those committed in principle to illegality still attach an inherited, Romantic importance to “the law as law.”
The class-conscious proletarian, however, must regard the question of legality or illegality as a purely tactical question, one that changes rapidly with circumstances.
The question must be answered, with complete “freedom from prejudice,” according to “considerations of immediate usefulness”—Lukács himself emphasizes those words.
Lukács too arrives at the antithesis:
The revolutionary struggle of the proletariat is “legitimate.”
At the end he says, literally:

“The proletariat of Central and Western Europe still has a difficult road before it. In order to reach consciousness of its historical calling, of the legitimacy of its rule, it must first learn to understand the merely tactical character of legality and illegality and rid itself both of legalistic cretinism and of the Romanticism of illegality.”
So there can be no doubt about the present importance of the distinction between legality and legitimacy.
Nor can there be any doubt that the title of my 1932 book, Legality and Legitimacy, was well founded.

But there can equally be no doubt that people who possess such dialectical clarity about legality and illegality will lose all sense of humour on this point once illegality is practised against them—once the illegality is directed against legal and therefore changing <…> .
In the otherwise remarkably complete chain of antitheses that Otto Veit constructs from the opposition between natural law and positive law, this particular antithesis is missing.
Why? Because the distinction between natural law and positive law is outdated.
Today that would produce, at best, a biological law—and we have all had quite enough of that.
Whether sacred history or history made by human beings.
History made ever more consciously, ever more deliberately, ever more according to plan, as historical consciousness and total planning grow in intensity.
History developing into the conscious and total planning of things to come.
